speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister indicated on June 1, the Lieutenant Governor of Quebec has transmitted to the Governor General, with favourable advice from the Government of Quebec, the Address to the Queen concerning the powers of the Legislative Council and the Address to the Governor General requesting him to transmit the Address to the Queen, with the assent of the Government of Canada, both of which were approved by the Legislative Assembly of Quebec on May 26. The Address to the Queen requests the passage of a new section 79A of the British North America Act to redefine the powers of the Legislative Council of Quebec.
I should now like to table copies of the Addresses of the Legislative Assembly to the Queen and to the Governor General; of the instrument of advice from the Government of Quebec to the Lieutenant Governor of Quebec; and of an exchange of letters which the Prime Minister subsequently had with Prime Minister Lesage to confirm that the Government of Quebec recommended action in accordance with the Assembly's Address.
To complete the outline of events to this date I may add that on June 8 the Governor General wrote to the Prime Minister asking for his advice as to the action he should take on the Address to the Queen.
In determining the nature of advice that it is the duty of the Government to give to the Governor General in this matter, the Government has given the most careful consideration to every aspect of what is a most complex and genuinely unprecedented situation.
The Address requests an amendment to the constitution of the Province of Quebec. Normally an amendment to the constitution of a province is made by provincial legislation under section 92(1) of the British North 22620-158
America Act. Indeed, the Government of Quebec sought to make the change in this way, but was frustrated in securing passage of the Bill by the Legislative Council, although the legislation had received the approval of the Legislative Assembly. The power of the Legislature to enact legislation under section 92(1) does not remove the jurisdiction of the British Parliament to amend the British North America Act itself, and it is such an amendment that is now sought by the Government of Quebec. The course proposed is entirely constitutional even though it is unprecedented.
Since there is no doubt as to the constitutionality of the course of action the Government of Quebec has recommended, the second question for our government has been the procedure it should follow with regard to it.
The proposed new section 79A of the British North America Act concerns only the provisions in that Act respecting the Legislative Council of the Province of Quebec. It affects neither the Parliament of Canada, the Government of Canada, the operation of the laws of Canada, nor any other province. The proposed change is in no way repugnant to the other provisions of the British North America Act. In short, this is a purely provincial matter of concern to Quebec alone. Because of these features, the proposed amendment is without any precedent in our history. We have never had an amendment to the British North America Act that concerned the constitution of only one province without concerning any other province, and which did not concern the federal authority.
The White Paper on Constitutional Amendment points out that a constitutional practice has developed that the sanction of Parliament is required for an amendment to the British North America Act. But that practice grew up in relation to amendments that concerned Parliament, the Government of Canada or the relationship between the Federal Government and the Provinces. What the Government has had to consider is how this practice relates to an unprecedented type of amendment.
The precedents with regard to amendment of the B.N.A. Act are listed on pages 11 to 15 of the White Paper on the Amendment of
June 16# 1965

Quebec Provincial Constitution the Constitution oi Canada which was tabled in this House on March 2, 1965. Hon. Members can readily confirm that not one of them was like the present one in being purely in relation to the constitution of one province. On those facts it is clear that the "principle" enunciated on page 15 of the White Paper, that the "sanction of Parliament is required for a request to the British Parliament for an amendment to the B.N.A. Act", does not apply to the present case.
For the same reasons it is equally clear that the opinion expressed by the House of Commons of 1871, as set forth on page 11 of the White Paper, does not apply. The House of Commons of that day adopted a resolution expressing the opinion that " ... no changes in the provisions of the British North America Act (would) be sought by the Executive Government without the previous assent of the Parliament of this Dominion". That view does not apply to a change sought by the Government of a Province relating solely to the Constitution of that Province.
Moreover, in a purely provincial matter of this kind, it seems to the Government that it would be wrong to act on a basis that appeared to suggest that Parliament could sit in judgment on the action of a Province within its own constitutional sphere. The Government has assumed that Parliament would not wish to do anything which would either deny the right of a Province to have its own Constitution amended in an entirely constitutional way, through amendment of the British North America Act, or to imply that the Federal Parliament has through an Address of the Senate and House of Commons the right or power itself to decide what the internal organization of a particular provincial authority should be. Apart from the office of Lieutenant Governor, those are matters which concern that province alone and not the Senate or House of Commons in Ottawa.
We have consequently come to the conclusion that the Government should advise the Governor General and, through him, the Queen to act in this matter in accordance with the advice of the responsible provincial Ministers, with whom alone the Government of Canada can properly communicate on matters relating to the Provinces as such. The Government of Canada comes into the matter because it has a responsibility to advise the Governor General and the Queen. The Canadian Government also must make the determination that there is not any aspect

of the proposed change that is of Federal concern. The Government has made that determination and intends to assume its constitutional responsibility of advising the Governor General and the Queen. The Government's advice will be favourable to the action requested for the reasons I have mentioned.
In case there is any doubt as to the propriety of revealing advice to the Crown before it is actually given, let me say at this point that, for ample caution, the permission of both the Governor General and the Queen has been secured to inform Parliament of the course that is intended.
To complete the elements of this complex problem that the Government has considered, let me say that the basic position of the Government would not differ as between an Address to the Queen from the elected Legislative Assembly and one from the appointed Legislative Council. The essential question in this matter which concerns Quebec only is the advice of the responsible provincial Ministers. The Government is satisfied, after an exhaustive study of the matter, that the course I have outlined is the right and proper one in an unprecedented and difficult situation.
However, in a matter of this kind the Government is not prepared to act formally until this House has a chance to express a view if it so wishes. In accordance with its opinion that this is a matter that concerns only the Constitution of Quebec, the Government does not propose to introduce any Address or Resolution calling for parliamentary action by both Houses. The Prime Minister stated on June 14 that the House would have an opportunity of expressing its views on this matter before any request was made of Her Majesty or of the British Government. Accordingly, to provide this opportunity the Government will be prepared to introduce a supply motion next Monday so that Members of the House may express their views on the course which the Canadian Government has decided to follow. No advice will be formally tendered to the Governor General or to the Queen until that opportunity for the expression of opinion in this House has been provided.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say at once that the only notice that we of the official opposition received from the Government that this matter would be brought up today was two minutes' notice in advance of the opening
June 16, 1965	COMMONS
of this House; when a copy of the statement to the press was, by the grace of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, given to those who would have to discuss it. This is but another example of an attitude on the part of the Government that is not in keeping with the traditions of Parliament.
I say at once that the alleged opportunity given to the House of Commons to discuss this matter by calling a supply motion on Monday next is an evasion of Parliament. It simply amounts to this, that the Government has not got the backbone to introduce a resolution in the House of Commons but wants to determine what shall be the amendment moved by the Opposition. This is a further step along the road of control that had its beginning when this Government took office and which it has followed since. Let the Government make its recommendation by an Address and bring it before Parliament.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
It has been said-my quotation may not be correct but it is to the point-
O. what a tangled web we weave,
When first we practise to deceive!
This certainly applies to the Government in regard to this matter.
What is this course that is being adopted?
I had the opportunity as the hon. gentleman read the statement to read it along with him, and I can summarize it in this way. This course is one that is dangerous to the Canadian constitution and its preservation.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: I am not arguing the question whether there should or should not be a second chamber in the province of Quebec.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Why not?

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
I have my own views with regard to the unicameral system and the bicameral system, but that is not the issue here.
Do you know what happened, Mr. Speaker, in this matter? Arrangements were made under the table between the Prime Minister of Canada and the Premier of Quebec; and if the Cabinet do not know about them they had better read what Mr. Lesage said as to the arrangements in the Legislature of Quebec. An arrangement was made between them in the spirit of what they now call co-operative federalism, which more and more is becoming a system of under the table arrangements, whereby the Prime Minister of Canada agreed
DEBATES	2481
Quebec Provincial Constitution to recommend to Her Majesty the Queen the acceptance of a resolution by one House of the Legislature of Quebec.
The Constitution clearly provides that the Legislature of Quebec consists of the Queen, the Legislative Council and the Legislative Assembly. That is the fact, and they agreed to this. They undertook to do whatever the Premier of Quebec wanted done, but they would not admit it in the House. I asked the Prime Minister, and he said there had been no agreement whatsoever and no arrangement whereby a resolution of one House, the Legislative Assembly, would be accepted and that recommendation passed on to the Crown. Having taken that stand-and I can quote from the Prime Minister's words- when finally it became apparent that this House would find out the fact and that the letter sent to Mr. Lesage would have to be produced, then the Prime Minister admitted that discussion in that connection had taken place.
This to me is a serious matter, and do you know what is behind it? It is the smiling Minister of Justice, the leader of the new guard. The leader of the new guard had to find a way whereby he could shove through the formula for the amendment of the Constitution. It was feared that as long as there was a Legislative Council he and those associated with him would not be able to force through the formula, and Mr. Lesage admitted that in the legislature. Something had to be done before the amendment formula was brought before the legislature, and the means followed were these. It first started with an address which passed the Legislative Assembly, was amended by the Legislative Council and then was withdrawn. It was realized that the hopes of the new guard, the old guard or the discards would not and could not be made effective, so they decided on a short cut.
Section 92(1) of the British North America Act provides that the Legislatures of Provinces have the exclusive power to amend the Provincial Constitution except as to the office of the Lieutenant Governor. This is an amendment of the Constitution of the Province of Quebec, and no amount of serious philosophy such as appears in the statement made by the Acting Prime Minister can get over this fact.
What is the legislature of Quebec? Under section 71 of the B.N.A. the legislature consists of the Lieutenant Governor and of two Houses, styled the Legislative Council of Quebec and the Legislative Assembly of Quebec. What is being done here? The Federal
June 16, 1965

Quebec Provincial Constitution Government, afraid to face Parliament by standing for what it states it believes, in a speech made today by the Acting Prime Minister seeks a devious and unconstitutional course so the Prime Minister's agreement with the Premier of Quebec can be carried out. Does this mean that the Constitution is to be turned aside when it is convenient to do so? The answer must be in the affirmative, and that is the reason the Government adopts this ludicrous proposal of promising to give the House of Commons the opportunity of debate, as set out in the statement:
Accordingly, to provide this opportunity-
That is, for the expression of the views of this House.
-the Government will be prepared to introduce a Supply Motion next Monday, so that Members of the House may express their views on the course which the Canadian Government has decided to follow.
Then, wrapping themselves in the garments of constitutional purity, these words were added:
No advice will be formally tendered to the Governor General or to the Queen until that opportunity for the expression of opinion in this House has been provided.
How nonsensical can a Government become, to use our supply motion in order to provide that opportunity. This Government has no backbone. This is another example of a Government that reminds me, as I have said on other occasions, of a cushion that bears on itself the marks of the last person who sat on it. They have been told what to do. They promised what they would do, and now they carry out the promise.
I mentioned the promise. The Premier of Quebec, with unusual frankness-and I have the Hansard here for those who would read- said it would be impossible to bring about the end of the Legislative Council if the formula to amend the constitution were accepted. In other words he is saying that we have a formula and we want to bulldoze it through, but we will not be able to get it through the legislative council. Therefore let us remove the legislative council's powers by a recommendation through the Government of Canada. This is playing ducks and drakes with the constitution simply because of the promise that was made by the Prime Minister to the Premier in the month of February. In other words, the fact that the Premier of Quebec has so stated indicates that he recognizes that once the so-called Favreau formula-

Fulton, Fulton.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: I am not trying to debate it; I am trying to throw some light on the nefarious conduct of this Government. If I were to debate it I would be quoting the precedents.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you are always very fair, but you certainly cannot be asking us to allow the Government to tell us what amendments we are going to move.
I have before me all the various instances that have occurred since 1867. I am not going into them except to say this, that the statement made by the hon. gentleman today to the effect there is no precedent that can be used is entirely without basis in fact.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: It is false.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Well, that is an expression you are not allowed to use in Parliament unless you belong to the Government ranks. I say this. If I were to argue the case I would refer to two instances in which the very reverse of what is being done here form the precedents.
I said a moment ago that this goes back to a promise, denied in this House by the Prime Minister when I asked him about it, but then when it became apparent that it would be revealed, he admitted it. Here is what Mr. Lesage said on May 11 as reported on page 2,441 of the debates of the Quebec Legislative Assembly, and I am translating from the French. "Without doubt", Mr. Lesage said, "I am going to read the text which has been written by Mr. Pearson and by me". Then it says, "The Prime Minister of Canada said that his Government, if the Legislative Assembly of Quebec approves the Address to the Queen which he proposes to submit
June 16, 1965	COMMONS
to it, this Address would be transmitted to Her Majesty with favourable notice-avec avis favorable"-my French may not be good, but my understanding of the words and the translation is good.
The promise was made. Now what are they going to do? They talk about colonialism, and then they take this over to the United Kingdom. They recommend, in effect, that it be accepted, in spite of the fact that the Legislative Council which is part of the Legislature of Quebec has taken a different view. What do they do? They place it on the doorstep of the United Kingdom. They place the Queen in the arena of party politics. I regret this action, but they would do anything to escape the consequences of the promise that ought not to have been made by the Prime Minister to the Premier of Quebec. The Address to the Queen is being used as a club by the Federal Government and the Government majority in Quebec to coerce one of the branches of the Quebec Legislature into assuring approval of the Favreau formula.
This is an action that I protest. I say that the statement made by the Minister today is a massive evasion and does not reveal the facts in so far as the constitutional development of our country is concerned, and constitutes an action that cannot be justified. It means that Premier Lesage agrees with us as to the freezing effect of the formula for amending the constitution, because afterward there cannot be any changes. I underline that.
Amendments to curb the powers of or abolish second chambers have been attempted before. I have before me, but I shall not read it on this occasion, an extract from the report of the committee of the Privy Council of Canada, approved by His Excellency on October 8, 1894, when the abolition of the second chamber in Nova Scotia was to take place. The decision in this case was as follows:
The Minister, in conclusion, observes that it Her Majesty's Government should think the circumstances sufficient to warrant so grave a step as their support to any amendment of the British North America Act, 1867, to enable the Legislative Council to be abolished by proclamation, it would seem to be quite contrary to the spirit of the constitution that such a proclamation should, at any time, be a measure for the consideration of Your Excellency, for the reason that such matters are not, according to the Constitutional Act, under the control or supervision of Your Excellency and your Ministers with regard to any of the provinces.
Finally they agreed years after, and the institution was abolished.
I take the strongest objection to this attitude on the part of the Government of play-

Quebec Provincial Constitution ing fast and loose with the constitution for political purposes, to carry out political promises that ought not to have been made.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first I want to protest having a matter as complex as this brought up on motions, with those who are expected to comment on it given no notice whatever about the nature of the statement which the Government was going to make.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
I received this statement which was to be made by the Acting Prime Minister just as I was coming down to enter the Chamber. I have had no opportunity whatever to peruse it, and it seems to me if the Government is going to make statements on matters that are of as far reaching importance as this, we ought to have some opportunity to look at these statements, and some warning in this regard.
Also Mr. Speaker, I want to protest against the suggestion of the Acting Prime Minister that this House should be satisfied to discuss the matter on a supply motion next Monday. This is becoming a very bad habit with the Government, of trying to sneak things in under some other item. Right now we are having the problem of the exclusion of certain American magazines amidst 18 other items in a budget resolution, and at times we have had $1 estimates to cover quite wide programs.
Now the Government is virtually seeking to get approval for an amendment to the British North America Act without consulting Parliament. When the Acting Prime Minister says we can have a debate on the motion to go into supply, may I point out that this involves a motion of confidence; that those who want to register their objection would have no choice but to defeat the Government; that if the supply motion should pass, in spite of the protests of those who may object to the subject matter under discussion, the Governor General in Council will still be the body that will be forwarding this proposed amendment to Her Majesty the Queen, and not the Parliament of Canada.
Not since 1871 has the executive ever sought to exercise the authority to recommend amendments to the constitution without consulting the elected representatives of the people of Canada. Why are we being asked to act as rubber stamps for this Government?

Quebec Provincial Constitution
There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, as to where this party stands with reference to the abolition of upper chambers. We do not want to become involved in any internal disputes in the Province of Quebec, but the constitution has to be complied with and there are procedures set down which ought to be followed.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
I am just going to explain, if the hon. Member will be patient. I would be glad to explain, but I am not sure that in giving my hon. friend an explanation I can give him the intelligence with which to understand it.
The Acting Prime Minister says the resolution passed in the Commons in 1871 does not apply. That resolution said that "no changes in the provisions of the B.N.A. Act would be sought by the executive government without the previous consent of the Parliament of this Dominion."

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
The Acting Prime Minister says that does not apply, as this has to do only with the Province of Quebec. In the next paragraph in his statement he says:
The Government has assumed that Parliament would not wish to do anything which would either deny the right of a Province to have its own constitution amended in an entirely constitutional way-

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: That is right.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: But, Mr. Speaker, the fact is that it is not being amended in a constitutional way.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Of course it is.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
If this matter pertains only to the Province of Quebec, then the Province of Quebec can amend its own constitution.
This refers to section 72 of the B.N.A. Act, and in 1941 the Province of Quebec amended the Legislature Act. It has the power to amend the act now without reference to this Parliament or to Her Majesty the Queen, but the reason it has not amended the Act is that the Legislative Assembly cannot get the concurrence of the Legislative Council. For that reason it is now asking the Government of Canada to forward an address to Her Majesty the Queen so that one section of the Legislature of Quebec may ask for an amendment.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: To do what the constitution says cannot be done.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
The moment that was sent to the Government of Canada the Government

of Canada had to decide whether it was going to forward it, but in our opinion the Government cannot forward it without submitting it to Parliament.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
So long as this matter can be dealt with by the Legislative Assembly of Quebec, then it is a Quebec matter; but the moment it is forwarded to the Government of Canada then it becomes a matter for Parliament.
When the Acting Prime Minister says we can have a debate on the supply motion I am sure he realizes that the debate would only be in this chamber. Is the other place to have no voice in discussing this matter? If this were to become a unicameral Parliament I would be very happy, but let us do it properly and not by ignoring the other place. I certainly hope it will not be too difficult to persuade the Government to use the same method to abolish the upper chamber in this Parliament that is being used to abolish an upper chamber in a province.
I think, Mr. Speaker, we have a right to demand that the Government, if it is favourable to the address passed by the Legislative Assembly of Quebec, bring that address into this Parliament. If there is to be a change in section 72 and the other relevant sections of the B.N.A. Act, then those changes ought to be contained in an address by the Parliament of Canada, not merely passed on by the executive without any reference to Parliament.
When I think of all the speeches hon. gentlemen opposite have made about having due regard for Parliament, and now they are going to recommend to Her Majesty the Queen by executive authority, a change in the constitution of Canada without any reference to Parliament Mr. Speaker, it does seem to me that this action will live to haunt the Government, revealing as it does the hypocrisy of all its pretensions about its devotion to Parliament.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Would the hon. Member permit a question? I know the hon. gentleman did not intend to say we were amending the constitution of Canada. What is being amended is that portion of the constitution which, under the constitution, remains the exclusive province of the Province of Quebec.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Oh, oh.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Even a layman like myself knows what humbug that statement is, Mr. Speaker. If this amendment is solely within the jurisdiction of the Province of Quebec, then the Province of Quebec can deal with it without reference to the Federal Government at all. The fact is that they are not able to do so because they cannot get the concurrence of the upper chamber. So they are seeking an amendment not to the Legislature Act of Quebec but to the British North America Act; and these gentlemen opposite who have talked about democracy and their devotion to parliamentary government are now proceeding to ignore Parliament and act by executive authority alone in making a recommendation to Her Majesty the Queen which in my opinion sets Canada back 90 years.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION

I contend that the Government has no right to make any recommendation to Her Majesty on anything affecting the constitution of Canada without the advice and consent of this House and the upper chamber.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have listened now for 45 minutes to a debate on this
DEBATES	2485
Quebec Provincial Constitution question. We in this group have given an attentive hearing, although I was not aware that a statement made on motions entitled the House to engage in a full debate. It seems to me that the same respect and courtesy we gave could be extended to us now.
I think it was unfortunate that the Acting Prime Minister did not make copies of his statement available to us before we entered the House; they were handed to us only as we came in to the chamber. maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS QUEBEC-ADDRESS TO HER MAJESTY RESPECTING PROVINCIAL CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
I cannot imagine this statement being prepared without the legal advisers of the Crown having given careful study to its contents. I believe we are dealing now with something which is certainly very rare as far as the Constitution is concerned, even if it is not altogether unprecedented. I think, therefore, the Government should have provided an opportunity for us to debate this question in circumstances other than those which arise on a supply motion. As I say, I do not think we are entitled to enter into a full debate on the issue this afternoon.
There is one point in the Minister's statement which impresses me. It is that this is purely a provincial matter of concern to Quebec alone. I believe this to be correct. Quebec is the only province in Canada which still has an upper house, and it seems to me that the organization of the structure of government within a province and the jurisdiction for which that Government should be responsible must belong to the elected Members of the provincial legislature.
I believe some Members of this House have been losing sight of a basic principle here. If this matter does concern strictly the Province of Quebec, then those responsible for decisions relating to the organization of Government within that province must be those who are elected as representatives of the people of Quebec. We live in a democracy. We say we believe in democracy. If that is so, then responsibility rests with those who have been elected to the assembly, provided always that the issue is strictly a provincial one.
The hon. Member for Burnaby-Coquitlam told us that never before had an amendment to the constitution been made without con-
2486	COMMONS
Quebec Provincial Constitution sultation with the people of Canada. However, this particular issue is one which relates only to the people of Quebec; and whether or not we agree with this action which has been taken in relation to the upper house in that province, it is the representatives elected by the people of Quebec who should have the say. I would say this is within then-constitutional authority.

I do not believe it is the constitutional right of the Province of Quebec to deal directly with the Crown, and therefore the transmission of their message- if they believe this is what should be done- should be carried out through the Federal Government.
I realize that the Minister's statement was made as a result of this problem having been placed before the Governor General, who approached this Government and asked for advice. This has been the advice. I believe it would have been much better for the Government to have sought the advice of Parliament, because I believe the transmission of such a request must be done through Parliament. Nevertheless, let us not lose sight of the democratic principle that the people of Quebec through their elected representatives have the final responsibility as far as this type of action is concerned.
I do not think we should prolong this debate further. Again I urge the Government to provide this House with an opportunity to discuss this issue in circumstances other than those which arise in connection with a supply motion. According to the Minister's statement a decision has already been made, so what is the use, after all, of bringing the matter before the House at all? It would do no more than provide us with an opportunity to state our various opinions. Still, it seems to me only reasonable that this subject should be brought before the House so that we may debate it in an appropriate manner.

May I mention that the person mainly responsible for the dilemma facing us today is the Quebec premier, because he has been elected to take care of Quebec's problems and he has no business transferring those problems to the Ottawa government, the London government, the Governor General or the Queen.
In two elections, he cried: "Masters in our own house"! But now he can no longer settle his own problems, having to place them in the hands of other governments, of the governor general and of the Queen, etc., etc.
It is a problem for Quebec, not for Parliament in Ottawa. It is none of our business, it is Quebec's business.
I was glad to hear, a moment ago, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) say that it does not concern us, that it is not our problem, and that is a fact. If the matter has been placed in the hands of the federal government the latter should send it back as quickly as possible to the government of the province of Quebec telling them to solve their own problems. I am sure that when the citizens of Quebec read in Hansard tomorrow that all of us here said in turn that it is none of our business, that it is Quebec's business, then the Quebec government will realize how humiliating it is for them to have asked someone else to settle their own problem when they could have settled it in Quebec.
The responsibility rests mainly on the Quebec Premier who was unable to settle a problem coming exclusively under Quebec jurisdiction.
Others are also responsible. Members of the cabinet, especially Quebec ministers, are responsible for the mess we are in. The petition was sent to the Governor General in order to be forwarded to the Queen. It was not sent to parliament. In these articles Dr. Gingras suggested that there has been an increase in limb deformities not associated with thalidomide, but he goes on to say that the Canadian Medical As-
Inquiries of the Ministry sociation's Committee on Maternal and Child Health has had its attention directed to the question as to whether or not there truly is an increase in this birth deformity.
Since the thalidomide tragedy of 1961-62 my Department has been engaged in two relevant areas of activity. Under the Health Grants Program three Prosthetic Research and Training Centres have been established to deal specifically with the problems posed by congenital limb deformities. One of these Centres is located in Montreal and is under the direction of Dr. Gingras. The deserved reputation of Dr. Gingras' Centre has no doubt resulted in an increased number of cases being referred to that Centre. We are inclined to give most weight to this explanation for the suggested increase, but Dr. Gingras' comment that other factors may be responsible will be pursued with him, as it relates to the efforts to improve our knowledge of the occurrence of congenital anomalies.
In addition, my Department, through its Expert Committee on the Occurrence of Congenital Anomalies, has been concerned with this very problem, that is, methods of improving our information about the numbers and kinds of congenital anomalies occurring in Canada. We are working with our advisors and the Provincial Health Departments in the development of a surveillance system for the purpose of detecting promptly any unusual occurrence of abnormalities. We are, of course, dependant upon the reporting of cases by individual physicians and I am, therefore, especially pleased to note the continuing interest of the Canadian Medical Association in this difficult problem.

Mr. Chairman, when the House adjourned last evening I was commenting on some features of paragraph 19 of the resolution before us and had made a direct reference to the so-called brain drain to the United States. I stated that I would comment on that feature in passing. Many of us have heard the expression used, "I don't think that the so-called brain drain to the United States is a one-way street. I believe we can get as much from foreign countries in mental development as we contribute to those foreign countries".
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
But of course Canadians are well aware of the great contributions Canadians have made to the building up of American institutions, and even to the American system of government. The late Mr. Lane, Secretary of the Interior in Woodrow Wilson's cabinet, was a Canadian from the Atlantic Provinces, a man often described as one who would have

made the presidency if it had not been for his birth in this country. There is Dr. Wallace Sterling, a man born, bred and raised in Ontario, a former professor in the University of Alberta, who is making a tremendous contribution to the educational life of the United States as President of the Leland Stanford Jr. University in Palo Alto, California, and most of us are aware of the great and beneficial career of the late Dr. Schurman who was raised and educated in the Maritime Provinces and placed Cornell University in the forefront of modern universities during his lengthy presidency. On the other hand we have men such as Dr. Wilder Penfield of the Montreal Neurological Institute. As I said earlier, I do not consider the brain drain to be a one-way affair.
But in the publishing business one has to consider the products of brains which are sold to the United States, even though the Canadians concerned may continue to reside in Canada. This is the problem which faces Canadian publishers. Not only do the brilliant writers and artists of this country move to the United States in large numbers, because of the greater market for their wares, but many of those who remain in Canada make their livelihood by selling to foreign countries, because of the better rewards they receive for their contributions as compared with those which Canadian magazines can afford.
I can give the committee one definite and striking case which remains in my memory. At the time of the thalidomide cases which were being discussed two years ago, one of the Canadian magazines ran an interesting article on this drug, its discovery, manufacture and use. The article went into these things in some detail. It was quite an interesting one and I learned considerably from reading it. Then a friend of mine suggested I purchase a United States magazine which also had an article on thalidomide and I went out of my way to secure a copy. I can only say that as a Canadian I felt very sorry about the superiority of the United States article as compared with the Canadian article. Indeed I was impressed to the point where I got in touch with the publishers of the two magazines. I found that the Canadian publisher had paid $750 for his article, which was all he felt he could afford. The United States publisher, on the other hand, had paid the brilliant writer who had written the article for him, $7,500. I do not criticize the Canadian publisher in any way. But when United States publishers are able to pay that kind

of remuneration for a good article, it is easy to understand why the editorial content of many United States magazines is superior to that of Canadian magazines.
I say, too, that Canadian magazines suffer from the brain drain to the extent that writers resident in Canada send their best pieces to the United States, and other countries abroad where they can receive higher compensation. Not only do we have this brain drain to compete against-and when I say "we" I am speaking from the standpoint of Canadian publishers. We have to consider the fact that if a United States magazine wishes to dump back on this country its editorial expenses such as the $7,500 for the thalidomide article, it can do so, and these expenses are spread not only over the magazine's circulation in the United States but also over its circulation in Canada. When the cost of an article is divided by this combined circulation the publisher will find it works out to a great deal less than the cost of an article to the publisher of a Canadian paper with a much smaller circulation restricted to this country. This is nothing but dumping. The entry into this country of magazines such as Time and Reader's Digest, their editorial content supplied almost entirely from the United States side, is a gross example of dumping.
Canadian consumer magazines are in trouble today; there is no question about that. The greatest obstacle to the successful conduct of Canadian consumer publication is the subsidized advertising rates offered by the nationally owned Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. In the United States market, magazines have to compete with television and radio stations, but at least the publishers know they are competing with private businessmen who must set advertising rates high enough to cover their operating costs and provide a profit. In this country, magazine and newspaper publishers are faced with Government subsidized competition from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation whose advertising rates need not cover the costs of the operation. If an advertiser refuses to pay the rates offered him, the C.B.C. will simply reduce them to any figure which will attract him. These rates need not cover the cost of operation, because subsidies provided by the Canadian public will make up any loss incurred. Canadian publishers have to establish rates which will attract advertisers to their pages in competition with Government-subsidized C.B.C. advertising rates on radio and
television, and this is not fair. Many Canadian publishers find they cannot secure advertising at rates which cover the cost of publication in the newspaper and magazine fields.
There are other angles in the business v/orld of the publisher which make one wonder at times whether the Government of Canada-and I do not mean this Government specifically; I am talking about governments which have come and gone over the last 20 years-is really interested in developing a Canadian publishing economy. I wonder how many people in Canada realize there are hundreds of foreign publications coming into Canada with a total circulation in the hundreds of thousands. Once these publications cross the Canadian border they do not pay anything whatsoever for carriage through the mails. This is due to a postal convention which operates on the theory that if a foreign publisher sends a magazine into Canada, a Canadian publisher presumably sends a Canadian magazine abroad. The result of this arrangement is that many hundreds of foreign papers come into this country by mail from Britain or France or the United States to addresses in Canada. The country of origin gets all this postal revenue, and once these publications cross the border into Canada we Canadians carry them free from their port of entry to wherever they happen to be addressed. Then the Canadian publishers are given the privilege of picking up the deficit by way of taxation to support the Post Office, which is carrying competitors' material free through the mails. I do not know any other business in Canada which is subject to this kind of competition, where a competitor is carried at your expense.
This situation has existed for many years. Canadian publishers have been protesting about it for years and years. We always get the same story: The Postal Union meets only once every five years; when the next meeting comes around we will fix this up. To my own knowledge these protests have been made for 25 years, now, and five meetings of the Postal Union have been held. But the Canadian Government has never yet straightened out this situation.
I should like to draw attention to the fact that the O'Leary Commission, reporting on the Canadian magazine industry, drew the attention of the country to the fact that these magazines and periodicals are carried free in Canada if they are mailed in a foreign

country to a Canadian address. On page 97 of the report of the Royal Commission on Publications we find the following:
The Canadian Post Office receives no revenue from the delivery of foreign second class mail because, under the terms of the Universal Postal Convention, all governments are required to handle free of charge whatever is passed to them by foreign post offices. The foreign post office retains whatever payment is made for the service.
The arrangement is reciprocal and therefore, in theory, equitable. Experience has shown, however, that between Canada and the United States theory fails completely in practice. Canadians receive far more second class material from abroad than they send abroad.
And the Royal Commission recommended:
That, in the matter of second class mail, the United States be asked for compensation in the form of terminal payments.
If American publishers were required to make terminal payments it would lighten the tax burden on Canadian publishers, who have to compete at present on such an unfair basis.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
But we have a practice in Canada which is known as the American remailing rate. The term is irregular, but it is known as that. Under this system approximately 60 United States publications, either by truck, express or freight send their periodicals into Canadian post offices, largely in Montreal and Toronto. While it is called the American remailing rate, it is better known as the American mailing rate, because they are not being remailed; they are being mailed for the first time.
Postage rates in the United States are so high, if a periodical is going to cross the international border and come into this country, that those who have a tremendous circulation have evolved a system, with the Canadian Government whereby, by sending the papers in bulk into Canada, they put them into Montreal and Toronto post offices and the Canadian Government collects a postage rate which is slightly higher than the Canadian publishers are asked to pay, but considerably below what these American publishers would pay if they had mailed in the United States.
Under this American mailing system the Canadian Post Office picks up about $900,000 a year. If the papers were mailed in the United States the Canadian Post Office would not pick up any revenue, so you might state that this $900,000 a year is better than nothing. But for the $900,000 a year that we now receive from American publications

coming in under the American remailing rate, it is estimated that the cost of handling those periodicals is in the neighbourhood of $2 million. So you have a direct subsidy to these 55 or 60 papers, through the American remailing rate, of about $1,100,000. And these are Post Office figures.
Canadian publishers have competition also with the Americans in the overflow circulation of the American pulp papers that come into this country. If you see Gordon's gin advertised in an American periodical, just because you are reading it in Canada does not mean that the advertisement has lost its effectiveness. If you see Johnson's wax, which is made at one place in the United States, and in Brantford in Canada, advertised in an American publication and you read it in Canada, the impact of the ad is not lost on the Canadian reader. You can buy Johnson's wax just as easily in Canada as you can buy it in the United States. But the manufacturers' reaction when these articles are nationally advertised in a Canadian paper is, "We have a 100,000 overflow circulation in Canada for which we do not have to pay a cent. Why would we pay anything to a Canadian periodical to carry our advertising, when we pay the cost of advertising to the American papers and the overflow into Canada makes it possible for us to reach our market without any additional cost to us?" Canadian publishers have to meet this obstacle of the overflow circulation.
In addition, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in its television programs attracts the attention of the public in viewing their programs. This also is paid for by the Canadian taxpayers, including the Canadian publishers. So the Canadian publishers have another opportunity to pay for their competitors with regard to the time they spend viewing this television advertising. The C.B.C. news service is in open competition with the news service of the Canadian Press, which was originated by Canadian publishers in about 1897 and is recognized the world over as a first-class news media. Why do we have to have a Government-subsidized news service running in competition with the Canadian Press, which has been built up at a great deal of expense to the Canadian publishers in this field?
Frankly, Mr. Chairman, I cannot support paragraph 19. It is an omnibus provision and I believe it should be split into sections. You will remember that the original flag motion when introduced into the House of Commons was split into two parts by the Speaker, and

I maintain it was rightly so split. Now we are asked to support paragraph 19, an omnibus clause which would allow Time and Reader's Digest to be classified as Canadian publications. I am not opposed to paragraph 19 if it applies equally to all bogus Canadian editions including Time and Reader's Digest. Steps have been taken to impede the entry into Canada of certain foreign publications, but bogus Canadian editions such as these two are to be granted separate permission. I say to you that making statements that this legislation is going to protect the Canadian magazine industry while allowing Time and Reader's Digest to be circulated in this country is the same as a farmer saying he is going to protect his chicken-house and he will shoot any fox that he sees, but he is not going to shoot the two foxes that are inside the chicken-house when he takes up his place at the chicken-house door with his shotgun. That farmer, if he had any sense, would clean out the two foxes that are inside.
The statement is made that if the advertisements in Time and Reader's Digest are taxed in such a way, the freedom of the press is involved. Freedom of the press is in no way involved. The publishers of these two magazines can send them into this country just as freely as the Financial Post, Newsweek, Atlantic and similar publications send in their copies. Freedom of the press is not involved in any way, shape or form.
The Canadian publishers are talking from the standpoint of dumping, and we are being subjected to this in every manner, shape and form by foreign publications. I have in my hand an editorial from the Ottawa Citizen of June 16, 1961. This is an article entitled "A magazine report" which was written just after the O'Leary Report came down. They pointed out that what is happening in the industry are unfair practices and they should be dealt with accordingly, for they are a form of dumping. That verifies what I have stated to you. This form of dumping in the Canadian publishing business has not been readily recognized by all Canadian businessmen.
This omnibus paragraph No. 19, would also, we are told, afford an umbrella type of protection to the Canadian owners of daily newspapers. I can only point out that with the exception of one daily newspaper in Canada, the other 103 have protested against this proposed action of the Government, and this proposed legislation. I am told by some people that a certain publisher in this country wrote a letter to the Government and said,

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry that there were some noes, because I always find the hon. Member for York-Humber very interesting to listen to, not simply because he is a maverick but because he discusses this particular subject of the publishing business well. I have something in common with the hon. Member for York-Humber in that I do not like this particular measure either, and I particularly object to the fact that we are dealing with an omnibus resolution which includes so many things in it. This is not just an ordinary resolution which deals with taxation matters; it goes much further than that. The question of Canadian nationalism and the type of feeling which should exist in this country in the future is involved, as one hon. Member mentioned last night.
We have heard a great deal in the last year or two about the nationalism of French Canada and the future survival of French Canada. I think that this is a similar situation for the country as a whole. What does it

take for a particular national or linguistic group to survive and to maintain the particular feeling which must be built up so that survival is possible?
There are many agencies in the country which are working at the idea of a national feeling. Certainly radio and television are two agencies which are very important in that respect. I suggest to you, Mr. Chairman, that if one were determined to wipe out French Canada, one of the things he would do would be to eliminate the broadcasting field entirely. In Canada we have taken deliberate decisions in the past to maintain, at quite great cost, a national broadcasting system. Complaints are made from time to time about how the system operates and how much its costs; but by and large, with very few exceptions, the majority of Members of Parliament reflect the view of the majority in the country that we must have this system for the survival of a Canadian national feeling in the future. We have a great many regulations designed to make sure that Canadian broadcasting is maintained, and we spend a great deal of money on the maintenance of this system.
I would suggest that our school system is another of the agencies which is used to maintain a feeling of Canadian identity-I am very much aware of this because before I entered this House I was a high school teacher of history and the social studies. In this field you work with whatever tools are available. You use textbooks. If popular journals are available dealing with Canada and various aspects of our history, then you use those as well. During my teaching career I have found that periodicals such as Maclean's magazine, Saturday Night and Weekend Picture Magazine were of considerable aid in this regard. If these were not available and we had to rely on United States publications, only, then would the task of the teacher be much more difficult. Therefore anything which strikes at Canadian periodicals I think endangers the type of feeling in our young Canadians which we wish to maintain in this country.
Let us take the case of Maclean's magazine. I have read it for many years. It has had its ups and downs. Sometimes it is good, sometimes not so good. I think it is on one of the down periods at the present time; nevertheless it is one of the best we have in the country. This magazine, published by the Maclean-Hunter Publishing Company, is subsidized by that company. They must take

part of the profits which they make from their trade publications in order to maintain the publication of Maclean's magazine and its French edition, Le Magazine Maclean. This company is a private enterprise. It is not a philanthropic organization. It is not a sort of Canada Council and it should not be expected to plough its profits from one side of its operations back into maintaining something which I think is essential for this country.
I do not suppose that many Members of this House would agree that the Canada Council or some other Government agency ought to give this company a direct subsidy to carry on with its work, but I think that the Government could take action to make the task of such companies a little easier at the present time. Certainly the proposed action of Canadianizing Time and Reader's Digest, thus depriving these Canadian periodicals of potential advertising revenue, is no help to them at all.
This has come about in a very strange way. I noticed one of the columnists in the Toronto Star, Mr. Robert Fulford, had this to say in his column on April 27, 1965, and I thought he summed up the situation very well. He said:
Canadian nationalism, as expressed by the federal government, is frequently more eloquent than rational. Consider the broadcasting regulations which limit foreign content on T.V. They were announced in 1960 as a means of promoting Canadian programs but instead the airways are today dominated by Hollywood to an extent few of us would have thought possible in the 1950s.
I realize that is another problem.

In this there is a kind of logic which is comprehensible only in Ottawa.

Regarding the proposal concerning newspapers, I think most Members of the New Democratic Party support the idea. This subject came up in New Zealand some time ago when there was a danger that one or two of the leading newspapers of that country were being considered for purchase by outside interests. The New Zealand Government at the time acted promptly to solve the problem.
I seem to remember from the history of the 1930's that there was some similar trouble in France, and that many of the newspapers of that country were effectively controlled, if not owned, by outside interests. I suggest that if United States publications were seriously threatened, this is what would happen, although that situation is not likely to develop in view of the growth which has taken place in that country and in view of its size and power.
Let us suppose the situation between the United States and Mexico was reversed and there was a gigantic Spanish speaking country of 190 million people living next door to the United States, and the power of that country threatened to dominate the smaller country next door. It has been said that this country was built in defiance of geography. It has been maintained in defiance of geography, living as we do next to a country which is so powerful.
