which is the third busiest airport in Canada serving the third largest metropolitan area of the country, is in a unique position. For the benefit of Members who have not had the good fortune of visiting the ever green playground, perhaps I can draw a comparison. If the airport in Toronto, that is the main International airport, were situated on Toronto Island and if that airport were connected to the city by a narrow, two lane
DEBATES	2511
Access to Vancouver Airport swing bridge which opened when tugs or barges came by, you would have some idea of the problem with which this particular area is faced. You can imagine the outcry that would be heard in the capital city of Ontario if, from time to time, this bridge were held open for a period of two hours while traffic was backed up for miles.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
The Vancouver International Airport is situated on a small island called Sea Island. Now, this island cannot be reached from the mainland, from the Burrard Peninsula on which the cities of Vancouver, Burnaby and New Westminster are situated, unless you go to another island called Lulu Island. You cross a bridge to that island, and then you cross a second small bridge to get out to the island on which the airport is actually located.
There have been problems in the past in connection with this bridge, Mr. Speaker. I have not kept a catalogue of the number of times the bridge has been out of commission and traffic has been held up. However, I should like to quote briefly from an article which refers to one of the worst examples of traffic being held up. I am quoting from the Richmond Review for April 19, 1962. The article describes the traffic tie-up which was caused by the failure of this bridge to function properly, and I quote:
Sea Island was cut off from Canada for 21 hours on Sunday.
A mechanical failure Is believed responsible for the jamming of the swing span on the Moray channel bridge. The bridge was opened for marine traffic, but refused to close completely.
While the defect was investigated, traffic backed up from the crossing to the airport. On the other side of the bridge, traffic piled up to the toll gates of the Oak Street bridge, where motorists were advised to take another route.
Incidentally, there is no other route to the airport.
Traffic flow was eventually restored before the fault was corrected, after traffic officials determined that the bridge was safe for traffic in spite of being two feet out of line.
Two flights were held up to allow delayed passengers to make connections. One, a Viscount flight to Edmonton was held up 40 minutes, and another Viscount to Victoria and Seattle was delayed 20 minutes.
Incoming passengers merely sat at the airport and fumed.
There is another heading in this newspaper which refers to the Liberals asking for quick action. The Liberal candidate for Burnaby-Richmond at the time commented on the situation and said that Ottawa ought to do something about it. He noted that Mr. Chev-rier, speaking in the House on this subject
June 16, 1965

Access to Vancouver Airport introduced by the previous Member for Burnaby-Richmond, had said something should be done about the situation. So, we have this problem, and I suggest that if the problem existed at Dorval Airport near Montreal or Malton Airport near Toronto, we would have heard a great deal more about it. The fact remains that the third busiest airport in Canada serving the third largest metropolitan area in Canada is tied up because of this bridge. This is quite important because of not only the possibility of delay for ordinary air line passengers, but the question of safety is involved. The main hospital in British Columbia is Vancouver General Hospital and it often has to receive people flown into the Vancouver International Airport from many parts of the Province. Someone may be seriously hurt in a logging accident. When he is flown to the airport, he has to get to the hospital as quickly as possible. If this bridge is out because of some passing marine traffic or because it has been hit by a barge, we have a very serious situation.
As I say, the problem is there and it has been there for several years. It is not a political matter so far as I am concerned. My predecessors who have represented Burnaby-Richmond, a Conservative and a Liberal, have both brought this matter to the attention of the House in the past. About a year ago the Federal and Provincial Governments did agree to undertake an engineering study to determine if a bridge or a tunnel were feasible at this point. The cost of this study was to be shared 50-50 by the two Governments. The report resulting from that study has not been published as yet, although I think they have had a great deal of time. Many local organizations are interested in this subject, as you would expect. The council of the municipality of Richmond, the Chamber of Commerce of Richmond, the Vancouver Board of Trade and the Sea Island Community Association, are all interested.
Recently the Richmond Chamber of Commerce wrote to the Deputy Minister of Transport about this subject. They wrote to the Minister of Highways in British Columbia as well. The reply from the Deputy Minister of Transport was dated April 29, 1965, and I quote:
With reference to your letter of April 23rd, addressed to the Minister of Transport and requesting a copy of the survey made on traffic flow from Vancouver to Sea Island, it is suggested that you direct your request for a copy of this report to the Department of Highways in Victoria.

While it is true that the cost of the survey is being shared equally by the Federal Department of Transport and the Provincial Department of Highways, the survey was initiated by and is being prepared under the direction of the Highway Department and, at the time of writing, we have not received the report on the second half of the study.
Then, they wrote to the Minister of Highways of British Columbia, Mr. Gaglardi. They received a reply dated May 7, 1965, and I quote:
This is still under study in conjunction with the City of Vancouver and necessarily has to tie in with urban street developments throughout the whole area. For this reason no final decision has been made and additional data is required before any further planning can be carried out.
Now, Mr. Speaker, some Members may wonder how the Federal Government becomes involved in this matter. Well, the airport is owned by the Federal Government and operated by the Department of Transport. Not only do they own the airport but they own almost 75 per cent of the land on this island. There remains on the island two residential subdivisions and a small amount of industrial area, but the largest part of the island is under federal control. I imagine that in the future, as we approach the day when supersonic aircraft will be operating, the Department will require more and more of the Island, so that eventually they will own it all. The Government is the owner of this property and administers the airport. The Government must feel some responsibility for making sure that passengers arriving at the airport from points in the United States, Latin America, Eastern Canada and Europe by direct flight can get off this small island and into the city or the surrounding municipalities. Similarly, people leaving Vancouver to go to many parts of the world should be able to leave without having to worry about a two-lane bridge that may be out of operation.
The Federal Government therefore is the owner of the property and the operator of the airport. For these reasons, I feel they have a definite responsibility to do something about access to the airport. I do not want to suggest the Federal Government has the entire responsibility. Generally speaking, bridges, tunnels and highways are a provincial responsibility. Certainly, the Government of British Columbia should accept some responsibility in this regard. The Government of British Columbia prides itself on the number of highways and bridges it has built. Those of us who live in the metropolitan-urban areas have a feeling the Gov-
June 16, 1965
ernment is rather more generous with other areas of the Province than they are with the more heavily populated lower mainland region from which they get the greater portion of their gasoline taxes.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
A year ago the Minister of Transport said that the Federal Government probably would not participate in the cost of building the type of connection requested here. He made some remark about the great big beautiful debt free Province of B.C. and that it could afford this itself. However, following that, the Department did agree to go 50-50 with the Provincial Department of Highways in the engineering survey.
Since that time the Minister of Transport has moved a little further. I imagine he has been prodded somewhat by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) who is a native of Richmond. His riding is on the Vancouver side of the area I am speaking about, and he has stated publicly and in letters to organizations that he feels such a tunnel should be built. He has had some success with his colleague, but not complete success.
The Minister of Transport was out there at the end of March, and he had this to say as reported in the Vancouver Sun of March 30, 1965:
Transport Minister J. W. Pickersgill said here today the Federal Government has made no decision on a suggestion that a tunnel be built between Vancouver International Airport and the city.
The Minister said in an interview studies are being made regarding better access to the airport, but no decision has been made as to whether a tunnel or a bridge or anything should be built.
"A study has been going on for some time, and a first report completed," he said.
"I will be studying that report when I return to Ottawa, and then a second study must be undertaken, presumably to determine cost."
Pickersgill was commenting on an announcement here last week by Northern Affairs Minister Art Laing that the government is considering construction of a tunnel.
The Minister said Laing was merely expressing a personal desire to see a tunnel built, rather than a bridge.
"I don't disagree with him that good access is needed to the airport," Pickersgill said, "but cost will be a large determination."
This problem becomes more urgent and there is the ever present danger of the bridge being out when it is needed at a vital time should an emergency arise.
Construction has begun on a large new terminal at Vancouver International Airport, and it is needed because there is increasing business there. I believe action should be taken now to begin the construction of a better access from the populous part of Van-22620-1601
Access to Vancouver Airport couver, and surrounding cities, to the airport.
The new terminal building is scheduled for opening in 1967. I doubt very much whether we can have a new crossing to Sea Island Airport ready at that time, but this very important decision must be taken quite soon. Between the time a decision is taken and plans are drawn up, and the time construction is carried out, a large amount of time elapses. Therefore I urge that the Minister of Transport ask his officials to conclude some type of negotiations with the Provincial Department of Highways on a cost sharing basis, so that engineering plans can be started and so that construction of this very necessary link be undertaken before many months pass.
The Minister of Transport said it all depends on the cost. If the Government admits it has a responsibility in this connection, being the owner and operator of the airport, then it has to bear part of the cost in agreement with the Government of B.C. I know agreement with B.C. may not be easily come by, but this is one of the tasks of government, to negotiate and obtain a proper cost sharing agreement so that the link from Vancouver to the airport can be begun and so that we will not suffer this ridiculous situation for many more years.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Davis (Parliamentary Secretary to Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
subsubtopic: VANCOUVER-CONSTRUCTION TO ASSURE ACCESS TO SEA ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a Member from the west coast I do not hesitate to endorse the general position taken by the hon. Member for Burnaby-Richmond Mr. Prittie) that we should have improved access from the built-up areas in Vancouver to Vancouver International Airport.
We read a good deal these days about the collapse of time and space. We know we can travel to any part of the world in a matter of hours, and it is a matter of some frustration to many of us that once we are grounded, once we are reduced to surface travel, the time elapsing between arrival at an airport and one's final destination is often comparable to that which one has spent in the air.
Some 50 years ago it took five days to cross Canada from Montreal to Vancouver. Today, even allowing for a half hour stop at Toronto, one can get from Montreal to Vancouver in approximately five hours. I do not want to imply that in a foreseeable period of time we will be able to span that distance in five minutes, but certainly if the supersonic air transport era arrives, in 10 or 15 years time it will be possible to get from Montreal to Vancouver non-stop in perhaps an hour and a half. For this reason delays

June 16, 1965

Access to Vancouver Airport on the ground become of increasing importance.
I would suggest that we as a nation can afford to invest much larger sums of money-in improving our avenues of surface transportation between the principal gathering points in downtown areas and the airport terminals. In this country air passenger miles have increased no less than fivefold over the last decade. This is a fantastic rate of increase. Air travel is relatively becoming more important than passenger rail travel, and is gaining on road transportation. Many more of the average Canadian's transportation dollars are going into air transport, and this is significant. We have some 5 million Canadian air passengers moving about the country each year. The proportion of the total population which is now flying from one point to another in Canada is substantial, and I submit is growing rapidly.
The sums of money involved in improving access routes to air terminals are not necessarily very large. They are certainly not large in relation to the sums of money being spent on subsonic, and in future years supersonic aircraft. They are not large relative to the sums of money being spent on the terminals themselves.
The tunnel which conceivably could be built under the north arm of the Fraser River, which would permit one to arrive at the Vancouver air terminal and 20 minutes later be downtown in Vancouver, might cost in the order of $6 million. This $6 million figure is small relative to the current investment Air Canada has in planes alone, which is something of the order of $300 million. This $6 million for the tunnel is also relatively small as compared with the estimated $23 million cost of the new air terminal building in Vancouver, which will be completed in our centennial year, 1967.
I suggest that if air pasengers had their choice they would put up with the present air terminal in Vancouver if they could get downtown in perhaps less than half the time, perhaps a third of the time that it takes them now to get from the terminal to the centre of the city.
I shall not attempt to describe the location of the proposed tunnel, because the hon. Member for Burnaby-Richmond has endeavoured to do that, but I would like to answer somewhat more specifically some of the points he has raised. In particular, he has asked for information.
Traffic circulation between the downtown Vancouver area and Sea Island on which the
International Airport is located, and the adjacent Lulu Island, has been a matter of considerable concern for a number of years. In view of the anticipated growth of airport operations as indicated in economic studies of the area-and in passing I may mention that the Stanford Research Institute recently completed a very extensive review of the Vancouver area-the situation can be expected to become acute within a short period, particularly as the present access to the airport is solely by means of one swing bridge which must also cater to the needs of the river traffic.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
In 1963 the Federal Government entered into an agreement with the Province of British Columbia whereby the Province would undertake a study and make a report on the feasibility and costs of a bridge or tunnel crossing the north arm of the Fraser River between the mainland and Sea Island. The Federal Government undertook to bear 50 per cent of the cost of such a study, such a contribution not to exceed the sum of $30,000. It was stipulated in the agreement that there was no undertaking, implied or otherwise, that the Federal Government would bear any of the cost of the construction of the crossing if it was built.
A firm of consulting engineers, Phillips, Barratt and Partners of Vancouver, appointed by the Highways Department of the Province of British Columbia did in January 1965 submit to that Department Part A of the Sea Island access study covering traffic forecasts and alternate routes. Part A of the access study was forwarded to the Minister of Transport by the Provincial Minister of Highways on March 23, 1965 requesting comments on the report. The Minister of Highways indicated he was prepared to initiate the second phase of the study concerning preliminary engineering and capital costs estimates for alternative crossings at Hudson Street, provided such action was agreeable to the Minister of Transport. In a reply dated April 14, 1965, the Minister of Transport here concurred in proceeding with Part B of the access study, namely the engineering cost study. In discussion with the officers of the Highway Department the target date for receipt of part B of the report from the consultants has been set for the end of September 1965.
I should like to summarize a synopsis of Part A of the report dealing with the traffic and the congestion expected to occur on the

June 16, 1965

present bridge access to the Sea Island airport. Both the Oak Street and Middle Arm bridges and their approaches are now loaded to their practical capacities, and during peak hour traffic flows their capacities are exceeded. This traffic growth will soon make conditions on the existing Middle Arm Bridge intolerable. A new four lane traffic facility, either a bridge or a tunnel, should be located across the North Arm of the Fraser River to accommodate the bulk of airport traffic which originates from or is destined to Vancouver. This location would not only represent the most direct route to Sea Island but would also help reduce traffic flows across the existing Oak Street bridge. The most feasible locations for this crossing are at either Hudson or Granville Streets. Department of Transport regulations, which limit obstructions on and in the vicinity of Sea Island, make a bridge crossing along the Granville Street route absolutely prohibitive. A high level bridge on the Hudson Street route is, however, marginally possible.
Later in the synopsis it is stated that in view of the many location, timing and cost uncertainties concerning the proposed Stanford freeway system for Greater Vancouver, it is not recommended that the new crossing to Sea Island be planned and designed as an integral part of a projected North-South Freeway. However, provision for a connection between a new Sea Island Crossing and a future North South Freeway can and should be made.
That is the position. The preliminary traffic study has been completed. It indicates there is an urgent need for either a tunnel or a bridge. It suggests that a four lane tunnel or bridge be built in the near future. The second phase of the investigation, namely engineering costs and related studies, is now under way and should be completed later this year. Obviously this is a subject which is of concern to the City of Vancouver and to the surrounding municipalities and, hence, to Greater Vancouver. It is of concern to several of the outlying municipalities which I represent-the districts of West Vancouver and North Vancouver, and the City of North Vancouver, which include among them the highest income municipalities in Canada. Their populations include people who travel a great deal more than most Canadians. They travel not only to different parts of Canada but to different parts of this continent and across the ocean, and in doing so they use airport facilities a great deal and are directly con-
Access to Vancouver Airport cerned with improvements in ground transportation.
The province, which is primarily responsible for highway construction, is obviously directly involved. However, I suggest that the Federal Government also has a responsibility in this connection. As a result of a transaction completed with the City of Vancouver a few years ago, it now owns the Vancouver International Airport. It is responsible for certain air force operations; and the Department of Transport operates on Sea Island. Moreover, the Department is primarily responsible for air transportation in this country and it must, therefore, concern itself with the physical facilities associated with such travel. In recent years, particularly in post-war years, we have done very well in respect to the vehicles of travel, such as aircraft. We have several very fine fleets which are relatively up to date. Air terminal facilities in this country are improving rapidly-I have in mind the airports at Montreal, Malton, Halifax and so on. We as federal taxpayers have invested more than $100 million in new construction to make it easier for passengers to arrive, board aircraft and be discharged from them.
I think a logical extension of this immense investment would be to take an interest in the access facilities to downtown areas so as to help people to travel more rapidly from these airports to their final points of destination. This calls for co-operation between the municipalities concerned and the Provincial Government, as well as between the Provinces and the Federal Government. In a very practical way I think we shall see another exercise in co-operative federalism in this field. I trust we shall see it at the Vancouver International Airport in the near future. I know we shall have a fine new air terminal in Canada's third largest and third busiest airport and I trust we shall also have by far the most efficient means of transporting passengers to outlying communities.
It is possible that a new tunnel-and I would certainly advocate a tunnel rather than a bridge-would enable passengers arriving at the airport to get to downtown Vancouver in 20 minutes. This would be a remarkable situation and a great improvement compared with the hour, or several hours sometimes, it takes to reach airports in other parts of the world from the centres of the cities they chiefly serve.
June 16. 1965

Access to Vancouver Airport
I, personally, as a private Member, intend to press for the construction in the near future of a $6 million four-lane tunnel under the North Arm of the Fraser River to speed up surface transportation to Vancouver International Airport.

subsubtopic: VANCOUVER-CONSTRUCTION TO ASSURE ACCESS TO SEA ISLAND
speechtext:
The resolution presented by the Member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) reminds us that in these days of rapid growth, one of the most difficult problems facing large cities is that of transportation. This is especially true of Vancouver because of the geographical features of the lower mainland. All motor traffic comes from the South or the East. The area we are now discussing and with which I am very familiar contains two islands, Lulu Island and Sea Island, formerly farmland but now largely subdivided into private homes occupied by people who work in Vancouver.
The suggested bridge or tunnel across the North Arm of the Fraser River would provide an alternate route for thousands of motorists during the morning and evening rush hours. We should remember, in this regard, that after the opening of the Oak Street Bridge several years ago the old bridge to Sea Island was demolished and never replaced. Another condition that merits examination is the fact that heavy traffic from and to the United States will continue to increase and create a bottleneck where cars leave the present bridge and enter Oak Street in Vancouver.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
However, the most compelling reason for the Federal Government giving favourable consideration to the resolution before us is the need of providing a second route to the airport on Sea Island. Today there is not only the possibility of inconvenience and delay for thousands of passengers, but the ever present danger of inability to deal with emergencies which may arise at any time. Surely it is the responsibility of federal authorities to plan ahead and to recommend facilities that will assure uninterrupted access in the future from Vancouver to the International Airport.

subsubtopic: VANCOUVER-CONSTRUCTION TO ASSURE ACCESS TO SEA ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see this resolution brought forward again this year. As the hon. Member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) mentioned in his opening remarks, the resolution was put on the order paper last year; it came forward and was debated. Now a year has rolled by and we are a little nearer

to having a new airport built in Vancouver, but there is still time to debate this resolution again.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, it must come as something of a surprise to you to learn that while we are on the eve of letting tenders to build a very large airport terminal in Canada's third largest city we have not yet settled the question of how to get to it. Here is the airfield where it has sat now for many years since the airport on Sea Island was taken up first for R.C.A.F. purposes and as a local airport, and it has expanded until now it has become one of the great major airports of the country. The question of how to get to this little island in the mouth of the Fraser is still a critical question, and is apparently still an unsolved question as we come right to the moment when we are about to build this air terminal.
One would expect, naturally, that the Province, which is responsible for the building of roads, and the municipalities, which are responsible for the building of local roads, would long since have taken up this question and we would not now have to be threshing away with surveys such as my colleague the Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister (Mr. Davis) mentioned in the course of his remarks, to determine whether to put a bridge and road through to this important airport. If the Province cannot get around to doing what the Province ought to do, supplying highways to the important points in British Columbia, I am sure the task will eventually fall back upon the Federal Government. The Federal Government will not let the people of Vancouver go begging one way or another, and will find some way of seeing that the road and the bridge are built.
If they do not, and these two jurisdictions are quite unable to do this, we will have a magnificent airport sitting out there on Sea Island and there will be no adequate access to it, except over the overcrowded Moray Channel approach. That will be a great day indeed for Okanagan Helicopters. This company, one of the biggest helicopter companies in the world, has its home base and head office on Sea Island, where this airport will be, and I am sure they would be delighted to lift all the passengers from the City of Vancouver to and from the airport if the Federal Government and the Provincial Government or the City of Richmond cannot figure how to get there by road or bridge.
When the hon. Member for Coast-Capilano, the Parliamentary Secretary, mentioned the
June 16, 1965

traffic that is growing on the Moray Channel bridge and which will shortly overcrowd that bridge, I reflected on how many times I myself had been held up going to and from that airport. One can recall the times not very long ago when the bridge, which is a swing-bridge, was opened to permit fishing vessels to go underneath. It is a narrow bridge. The road must converge at that point into one single stream of traffic in either direction in order for one to reach the airport or to come back from the airport. So that traffic cannot move very swiftly. Unless you hit it at rush hours, it is not too inconvenient; but at rush hours the traffic may back up until it is standing for several blocks in either direction waiting to get across the Moray Channel bridge. And at times when there is really some great occasion to move out to the airport, such as for a reception for some great person who comes to visit Vancouver, or something of this kind, then the road is plugged completely and vehicles stand there with the drivers pumping on their horns and hoping against hope that the traffic will move, wondering whether they will get home for dinner or whether they will have to camp out. So it is most important indeed that this matter be taken up along with the question of building a new airport at Vancouver.
While I am on this subject, Mr. Speaker, I want for a moment to digress. This is an hour of the day in which digressions seem to occur, and perhaps Your Honour will permit a digression in connection with the building of an airport at Vancouver. A number of us in Vancouver have been taking up with the Minister the question of airport art. As you know, it is the custom today to put into all the new airports in Canada some contentious art work. In the airport at Edmonton there is a great splash of a mural on the wall which looks as if an aircraft had "pranged" there.

In the new airport at Regina, I think it is, they have some children's blocks placed upon the wall, painted in different colours, as children's blocks generally are, and that looks quite interesting. In the airport at Winnipeg they have some bars up and down and a few of them across, and that is a very interesting design indeed. I am sure an artist of great renown built that and sold it to the Department of Transport at a considerable price. In the airport at Toronto they have some rather different things. This shows the broadness of our national culture.
Access to Vancouver Airport There on a steel pole one can see several shafts or rods pointing in different directions, which gives one a bit of a feeling of flight. However, if flight should fail you can go down to the other end of the airport and there you can find what might be best described as junkyard art. This is that field of sculpture which embraces such things as old, cast-off engine blocks and things like that which have been moulded into some pleasant and appealing pattern. They have one or two of these in that airport.
We in Vancouver, Sir, thought a little differently about this. We had a notion, strange and antique though it might be, that we would like to see something representative of the culture and work of the coast. We thought in terms perhaps of some of the magnificent trees, and so on, which grow in our forests and which adorn many of our buildings and public edifices in Vancouver. We thought of our magnificent mountains; we thought of some of the great Indian art which has become a part of the culture and the heritage of the coast, and we went to the Minister and officials of the Department of Transport. I went along with other people from Vancouver interested in this matter to see them about it. Sir, we met with considerable resistance. No one really wanted to think that when you alighted in a city like Vancouver you should be unnerved by a regional feeling. The thought was that you should get a grip on the whole of Canada, as it were, as you stepped into the airport and should not see just the great mountains of the Pacific, the feeling of our forests, our woods and so on. But like that aircraft which "pranged" at Winnipeg, or those twisted engine blocks you can see at Toronto, you have a feeling of the whole country from junkyard to junkyard, from city to city, from Atlantic to Pacific. So we badgered them to some considerable extent. Gradually I felt some life was creeping into the Ministry and that, indeed, they might listen to us. I had hoped that when this airport was finished and the gates were opened you could go there and find, to the astonishment and dismay of art circles from coast to coast, something which you could recognize and which suggested to you that this is the great and broad country of the Pacific, something which we could all understand and appreciate.
[DOT] (5:40 pm.)
Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, this is a digression which you will permit me, but I will try to return in a moment to the topic at hand. This
June 16, 1965

Access to Vancouver Airport airport is important not only as the western terminus of Air Canada, not only as the home and base of a great commercial helicopter company, to which I referred a moment ago; it is also the head office and central terminal of Canadian Pacific Air Lines. I was very interested to hear the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) announce in the House a few days ago the new policy for dividing the overseas operations of Air Canada and Canadian Pacific Air Lines into regions. As far as Canadian Pacific Air Lines is concerned, which will very shortly be a world girdling air line, one of the very few, its head office and base will be at this very airport to which we find such difficulty of access today. It will be bringing passengers and cargo from the Orient, from South America and from around the world through its head office and through this airport at Vancouver.
It is for this reason, as well as for the reason of serving other major Canadian air lines such as Air Canada and the local air lines which serve the interior of the province, that we need in Vancouver more than a single lane for traffic travelling in each direction to and from this airport. This is why it is essential that the planning of this access gets under way concurrently with the planning of this great terminal, so that when the gates of the terminal are opened we do not find ourselves as frustrated as we have been in the past with the inadequate road and bridge accommodation which is provided today.
I think that these remarks, brief and divergent though they may be, may give the House some idea of the importance of this issue and why my hon. friend from Burnaby-Richmond has seen fit to bring the question back in the form of the motion now before the House this day. I hope that this debate, which will be recorded in Hansard, will be read by the Minister, and indeed, more than that, will even be read by Mr. Gaglardi, the Minister of Highways of the Province of British Columbia, whose magnificent roads stretch almost everywhere except in adequate size to Sea Island, where we need a road, bridge and a new airport.

subsubtopic: VANCOUVER-CONSTRUCTION TO ASSURE ACCESS TO SEA ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to hear a government member telling us how much he appreciates the efforts of a Social Credit minister of British Columbia in order to carry out splendid projects in road construction. I see the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Pepin) applauding. This shows perhaps

that, like us, he appreciates highly the work done by the Social Credit government in British Columbia.
Mr. Speaker, the object of the notice of motion of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Prittie) is the building of a bridge or a tunnel across the North arm of the Fraser River between the City of Vancouver and Sea Island in the municipality of Richmond for the purpose of assuring uninterrupted access to the Vancouver International Airport.
In my opinion, this request is far from being extravagant. It is realistic and very worthwhile. I think the house should pass the motion right away, because it is not a matter of politics or partisanship; on the contrary, it is a question of giving to a province a service of which it was deprived up to now.
We are not well acquainted with British Columbia and this is something which is not done in the province of Quebec in spite of the fact that we have already asked for a bridge or tunnel between Quebec City and Levis. We have no objection to the construction of a bridge or a tunnel within the limits of British Columbia. The hon. member is certainly right and his notice of motion was undoubtedly submitted as a result of requests from his constituents and citizens of Vancouver or people living in the vicinity of the Vancouver airport.
Mr. Speaker, we heartily support this motion and we hope that members of the government will not object to the building of a bridge or tunnel-whatever is the cheapest, because the burden of Canadian taxpayers is heavy enough as it is-in order to serve adequately the people from this area of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, since it is 5.50 p.m. and our group does not wish to prevent the passage of this notice of motion or the carrying out of this project, I shall speak no further.
Before resuming my seat, I shall merely add that we fully endorse the request of the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond.

It should not be forgotten, as so often it
is, Mr. Speaker, that Vancouver and the lower mainland of British Columbia is only part of that Province; that is, British Columbia consists of something more than just the lower mainland and Vancouver. Other expenditures are required in areas where the wealth of that Province is actually developed. In this regard there is a requirement for great expenditures on the part of the Provincial and Federal authorities in order to carry out joint programs. I would have thought that this matter, together with many others, would have been an excellent subject for discussion by the representatives from British Columbia, if not at the Dominion-Provincial Conference itself, at least with others here in Ottawa when the British Columbia Cabinet members and the officials are here attending that Conference. Mr. Speaker, that is a typical expression of Social Credit philosophy: Anything that is physically possible is economically feasible. That may or may not be so, 22620-161
Access to Vancouver Airport but so far in this discussion I have not said that the proposed project is not justifiable.
Let me assure the hon. Member that if the Premier and the Cabinet of the Province of British Columbia were more co-operative and assisted us at least in informing the general public as to the amounts of expenditures the Federal Government makes in respect of joint programs, and in respect of direct grants, it would be helpful, but this co-operation is singularly lacking on the part of the Cabinet of the Province of British Columbia. I think every Member, whether he is a politician or a statesman, must and does realize that under our system of responsible Government, and no one knows this better than the Cabinet of the Province of British Columbia, when an expenditure is made by a body that has collected the taxes, that body should at least receive some credit. It should be shown that the contributing body is contributing, otherwise our system of responsible Government breaks down, and I refer particularly to the federal system.
I should like to give one example of the lack of co-operation in this regard, and this refers to something which took place while the Conservative Party was in power here in Ottawa. On the completion of a section of the Trans-Canada Highway through a very mountainous section of the Rockies and Cascades, which had received great publicity, the Federal Government planned a joint Federal-Provincial grand opening ceremony. The Provincial Government rushed ahead and conducted an opening ceremony two weeks ahead of the planned joint opening. The joint financial arrangements for the construction of this section of the highway provided that the Federal Government would contribute 90 per cent of the cost of 10 per cent of the highway, plus 100 per cent of the cost of construction of the highway through Western National Parks. As a result of this the Federal Government spent almost $100 million, whereas the Provincial Government spent $2,700,000. That is an example of the lack of co-operation on the part of the British Columbia Cabinet, and that is why I say that at least in respect of joint programs the provincial governments should co-operate in a small measure by informing the general public as to the source of this money.
